স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১) Drugs causing acute colonic pseudo-obstruction
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Opiates (opioids) are a common drug cause of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie’s syndrome) due to inhibition of intestinal motility.

Mechanism:

  • Opioids stimulate μ-opioid receptors in the gut

  • ↓ Acetylcholine release in the enteric nervous system

  • ↓ Peristalsis → colonic dilatation without mechanical obstruction

Other drugs associated with pseudo-obstruction:

  • Anticholinergics

  • Calcium channel blockers

  • Antipsychotics

  • NSAIDs: Not a typical cause of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction.

  • SSRIs: Can affect GI motility but are not classic causes.

  • TCAs: May cause constipation due to anticholinergic effects, but less classically linked than opioids.

Exam Pearl:
Drug-induced acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) → Opioids.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ২) Complications that can arise from both acute and chronic pancreatitis
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Pancreatic pseudocyst formation is a complication that can occur in both acute and chronic pancreatitis.

Mechanism:

  • In pancreatitis, leakage of pancreatic enzymes and fluid causes a collection of pancreatic fluid surrounded by fibrous tissue (without an epithelial lining) → pseudocyst.

  • It may occur after acute pancreatitis and is also common in chronic pancreatitis.

  • Hyperglycaemia: More commonly associated with chronic pancreatitis due to pancreatic endocrine insufficiency (Type 3c diabetes), not a typical complication of acute pancreatitis.

  • Hypercalcaemia: Not a complication; rather, hypercalcaemia is a cause of pancreatitis.

  • Septicaemia: Can occur in severe necrotizing pancreatitis, but not a characteristic complication of both forms.

Exam Pearl:
Acute + chronic pancreatitis common complication → Pancreatic pseudocyst.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ৩) Gastric and duodenal ulcer can be differentiated from erosion on the basis of penetration into
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
The key difference between an ulcer and an erosion is the depth of mucosal injury.

  • Erosion: A superficial mucosal defect that is limited to the lamina propria and does not cross the muscularis mucosa.

  • Ulcer (gastric/duodenal): A deeper defect that penetrates through the muscularis mucosa and extends into deeper layers (often the submucosa or muscularis propria).

Therefore, penetration beyond the muscularis mucosa differentiates an ulcer from an erosion.

  • Lamina propria: Site involved in erosion.

  • Submucosa: May be involved in deeper ulcers but is not the defining boundary.

  • Muscularis propria: Deep penetration; may occur in complicated ulcers.

Exam Pearl:
Erosion = does not cross muscularis mucosa; Ulcer = crosses muscularis mucosa.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ৪) Best screening test for acute hepatitis B infection
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
The best screening test for acute hepatitis B infection is IgM anti-HBc (IgM antibody against hepatitis B core antigen).

Reason:

  • IgM anti-HBc appears early during acute HBV infection.

  • It indicates recent infection and remains positive for several months.

  • It is especially useful during the window period, when HBsAg has disappeared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared.

  • HBsAg: Indicates current HBV infection (acute or chronic) but cannot reliably distinguish acute from chronic infection.

  • HBcAg: Not routinely detected in serum because it is present inside hepatocytes.

  • IgM anti-HBe: Not used as a diagnostic marker for acute HBV infection.

Exam Pearl:
Acute hepatitis B → IgM anti-HBc is the best marker.
HBsAg = infection marker; IgM anti-HBc = acute infection marker.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ৫) Cardinal finding in portal hypertension
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
The cardinal (most important clinical) manifestation of portal hypertension is variceal bleeding, especially oesophageal variceal haemorrhage.

Portal hypertension causes:

  • Increased portal venous pressure → formation of portosystemic collaterals

  • Most clinically significant collateral sites are oesophageal veins

  • Rupture of varices can cause massive upper GI bleeding

  • Splenomegaly: Common finding due to congestive splenic enlargement, but not the cardinal complication.

  • Ascites: Common in advanced portal hypertension due to fluid accumulation.

  • Renal failure: Occurs as a complication in advanced liver disease (hepatorenal syndrome).

Exam Pearl:
Portal hypertension → Oesophageal varices → Variceal bleeding (most serious/cardinal manifestation).

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ৬) Which is the best means of detecting ascites
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Ultrasonography (USG) is the best initial and most sensitive method for detecting ascites, especially small amounts of free fluid.

Advantages of USG:

  • Detects even minimal ascitic fluid

  • Non-invasive and radiation-free

  • Easily available and cost-effective

  • Helps guide diagnostic paracentesis

  • X-ray: May show signs of large ascites (e.g., increased abdominal density), but is not sensitive.

  • CT scan: Can detect ascites and provide additional abdominal details, but is not the first-line test.

  • MRI: Not routinely used for ascites detection.

Exam Pearl:
Best investigation for detecting ascites → USG.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ৭) Electrolyte and acid base status in GOO can be described as
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Gastric outlet obstruction (GOO) causes persistent vomiting of gastric contents, leading to loss of hydrochloric acid (HCl) from the stomach.

Mechanism:

  • Loss of H⁺ ions → metabolic alkalosis

  • Loss of Cl⁻ ions → hypochloraemia

  • Volume depletion activates RAAS → increased renal bicarbonate retention, worsening alkalosis

  • Potassium loss may cause hypokalaemia

  • Hypochloraemic metabolic acidosis: Not seen in vomiting; occurs with bicarbonate loss (e.g., diarrhoea).

  • Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis: Seen in renal tubular acidosis or diarrhoea.

  • Hyperchloraemic metabolic alkalosis: Not a typical pattern.

Exam Pearl:
Persistent vomiting / Gastric outlet obstruction → Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ৮) Investigation of choice for GERD
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
The investigation of choice for diagnosing GERD is 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring. It is the gold standard test for detecting abnormal oesophageal acid exposure and confirming gastro-oesophageal reflux.

It measures:

  • Frequency of acid reflux episodes

  • Duration of acid exposure

  • Correlation between symptoms and reflux events

  • Upper GI endoscopy: Used to detect complications of GERD such as oesophagitis, Barrett’s oesophagus, strictures, and malignancy; not the most sensitive diagnostic test for uncomplicated GERD.

  • Urea breath test: Used for H. pylori infection detection.

  • Oesophageal manometry: Assesses oesophageal motility and is useful before anti-reflux surgery, not for primary diagnosis.

Exam Pearl:
GERD diagnosis → 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring (gold standard).

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ৯) Which antibody is frequently present in primary biliary cholangitis
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is strongly associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), especially AMA-M2 subtype, which is present in about 90–95% of patients.

PBC features:

  • Chronic autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts

  • Middle-aged women commonly affected

  • Cholestatic liver disease → ↑ ALP, pruritus, jaundice

  • Anti-dsDNA antibody: Associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

  • Anti-smooth muscle antibody: Associated with autoimmune hepatitis type 1.

  • Anti-microsomal antibody (anti-TPO): Associated with autoimmune thyroid disease (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves’ disease).

Exam Pearl:
PBC → Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA-M2).
Autoimmune hepatitis → Anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA).

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১০) In which disease ‘Onion skin’ fibrosis is found in liver biopsy
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
“Onion skin” fibrosis on liver biopsy is a classic histological feature of Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

Mechanism:

  • PSC causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.

  • This leads to concentric periductal fibrosis around bile ducts, producing an “onion-skin” appearance.

Associated features:

  • Strong association with ulcerative colitis (UC)

  • Cholestatic liver enzyme pattern (↑ ALP)

  • Risk of cholangiocarcinoma

  • Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): Shows destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts with florid duct lesions and granulomatous inflammation; associated with AMA.

  • Wilson’s disease: Copper accumulation with chronic liver damage.

  • Haemochromatosis: Iron deposition causing cirrhosis and pigmentation.

Exam Pearl:
Onion-skin periductal fibrosis → Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১১) Most common cause of chronic or relapsing diarrhoea
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
The most common cause of chronic or relapsing diarrhoea is Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), particularly diarrhoea-predominant IBS (IBS-D).

Features of IBS:

  • Chronic or recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits

  • Diarrhoea and/or constipation

  • No structural or inflammatory abnormality

  • Symptoms often fluctuate and relapse

  • IBD (Inflammatory Bowel Disease): Causes chronic diarrhoea but is less common than IBS and usually has inflammatory features (blood, weight loss, raised inflammatory markers).

  • Entamoeba infestation: Causes amoebic dysentery, usually with blood and mucus in stool.

  • Giardiasis: Causes chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption but is less common.

Exam Pearl:
Commonest cause of chronic relapsing diarrhoea → IBS.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১২) Severe, constant upper abdominal pain of increasing intensity over 15-60 minutes which radiates to the back is the typical presentation of
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Severe, constant upper abdominal (epigastric) pain that increases in intensity over 15–60 minutes and radiates to the back is the classic presentation of acute pancreatitis.

Typical features:

  • Sudden onset severe epigastric pain

  • Radiation to the back due to retroperitoneal pancreatic inflammation

  • Pain may be relieved by leaning forward

  • Associated with nausea, vomiting, and raised serum amylase/lipase

  • Gut perforation: Causes sudden severe abdominal pain with peritonitis and a rigid abdomen; pain is not typically radiating to the back.

  • Intestinal obstruction: Causes colicky abdominal pain with vomiting and abdominal distension.

  • Chronic pancreatitis: Causes recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back but is usually less acute and associated with chronic features (malabsorption, steatorrhoea).

Exam Pearl:

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১৩) Which hepatitis virus cannot be prevented by vaccine
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Currently, there is no effective vaccine available for Hepatitis C.

Reason:

  • HCV has high genetic variability due to frequent mutations, making vaccine development difficult.

  • Prevention relies on:

    • Screening of blood products

    • Safe injection practices

    • Avoiding exposure to infected blood

  • Hepatitis A: Vaccine available (inactivated HAV vaccine).

  • Hepatitis B: Vaccine available (recombinant HBsAg vaccine).

  • Hepatitis D: No separate vaccine, but it is prevented by Hepatitis B vaccination because HDV requires HBV for replication.

Exam Pearl:
No vaccine → Hepatitis C.
HBV vaccine also prevents HDV infection

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১৪) Most common cause of acute pancreatitis
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
The most common cause of acute pancreatitis is gallstone disease (biliary pancreatitis).

Mechanism:

  • A gallstone may obstruct the ampulla of Vater → blockage of pancreatic duct outflow

  • Pancreatic enzyme activation occurs inside the pancreas → autodigestion and inflammation

Common causes of acute pancreatitis (GET SMASHED):

  • Gallstones ✅

  • Ethanol (alcohol)

  • Trauma

  • Steroids

  • Mumps (and other infections)

  • Autoimmune

  • Scorpion sting

  • Hypercalcaemia / hypertriglyceridaemia

  • ERCP

  • Drugs

  • Alcohol: One of the most common causes, especially in Western countries, but overall gallstones are most common.

  • Idiopathic: Diagnosis when no cause is found, but less common.

  • Post ERCP: Recognized cause but uncommon.

Exam Pearl:
Commonest cause of acute pancreatitis → Gallstones.
Commonest cause of chronic pancreatitis → Alcohol.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১৫) Which hepatitis virus doesn't develop chronicity
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Hepatitis A does not develop chronicity. HAV infection is an acute, self-limiting hepatitis and does not lead to chronic hepatitis or a carrier state.

Key points:

  • Spread: Feco-oral route

  • Causes acute hepatitis only

  • No chronic infection or cirrhosis

  • Vaccine is available

  • Hepatitis B: Can become chronic, especially when infection occurs in neonates and young children.

  • Hepatitis C: Has a high risk of chronicity (around 70–80% of infections).

  • Hepatitis D: Can cause chronic infection when associated with HBV.

Exam Pearl:
Hepatitis virus that does NOT cause chronic hepatitis → Hepatitis A.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১৬) Dyspepsia in patients over 55 or with alarm symptoms demands
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Dyspepsia in patients aged >55 years or with alarm symptoms requires upper GI endoscopy (OGD) to exclude serious pathology such as gastric cancer, oesophageal cancer, peptic ulcer disease, or complications.

Alarm symptoms include:

  • Dysphagia

  • Odynophagia

  • Unintentional weight loss

  • GI bleeding (haematemesis/melaena)

  • Iron deficiency anaemia

  • Persistent vomiting

  • Palpable mass or lymphadenopathy

  • USG: Useful for hepatobiliary causes but not the investigation of choice for dyspepsia.

  • ECG: Used for cardiac causes of chest pain, not dyspepsia evaluation.

  • CT: Not first-line; used when complications or malignancy staging is suspected.

Exam Pearl:
Dyspepsia + age >55 or alarm features → Upper GI endoscopy (OGD).

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১৭) Structures that can be seen in upper GI endoscopy except
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) is used to visualize the upper gastrointestinal tract, including:

  • Oesophagus

  • Stomach

  • 1st part of duodenum (D1)

  • 2nd part of duodenum (D2)

The pharynx is not routinely examined as part of upper GI endoscopy because the scope passes through the pharynx but does not provide a detailed evaluation of it.

  • Stomach: Clearly visualized in OGD.

  • 1st and 2nd parts of duodenum: Visualized during routine upper GI endoscopy.

Exam Pearl:
OGD visualizes → Oesophagus + Stomach + D1 + D2.
Pharynx is not a target structure.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১৮) Which can confirm acute pancreatitis
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
Serum lipase is the preferred biochemical test to confirm acute pancreatitis.

Why lipase is preferred:

  • More specific for pancreatic injury than amylase

  • Remains elevated longer (7–14 days) after onset

  • Less affected by non-pancreatic conditions

Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis requires 2 of 3 criteria:

  1. Typical abdominal pain (epigastric pain radiating to back)

  2. Serum lipase/amylase ≥3 times normal

  3. Imaging evidence of pancreatitis

  • Amylase: Also rises in acute pancreatitis but is less specific and normalizes earlier.

  • USG: Useful to detect gallstones and biliary cause, but not the best confirmatory test.

  • ERCP: Used mainly for biliary obstruction/cholangitis, not diagnosis.

Exam Pearl:
Best confirmatory enzyme for acute pancreatitis → Serum lipase.

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ১৯) Most common cause of acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
The most common cause of acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage (UGI bleeding) is peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

Mechanism:

  • Peptic ulcers erode into underlying blood vessels (especially the gastroduodenal artery in duodenal ulcers), causing haematemesis or melaena.

Common causes of acute UGI haemorrhage:

  1. Peptic ulcer disease ✅

  2. Oesophageal/gastric varices

  3. Gastritis/duodenitis

  4. Mallory–Weiss tear

  • Gastric erosion: Can cause bleeding but is less common than peptic ulcer.

  • Oesophagitis: Usually causes minor bleeding, not the commonest cause.

  • Vascular malformation: Can cause bleeding but is less frequent.

Exam Pearl:
Most common cause of acute upper GI bleeding → Peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

স্পেশাল কুইজ.question: ২০) Test to demonstrate anatomy of pancreas prior to surgery
স্পেশাল কুইজ.exp:
MRCP is the preferred non-invasive investigation to demonstrate the anatomy of the pancreas and pancreatic ductal system prior to surgery.

Advantages of MRCP:

  • Non-invasive

  • Provides detailed images of the pancreatic duct, biliary tree, and anatomical variations

  • Useful for surgical planning (e.g., pancreatic surgery)

  • ERCP: Provides detailed duct imaging but is invasive and mainly used for therapeutic procedures (stone extraction, stenting), not routine preoperative anatomical assessment.

  • USG: Useful as an initial imaging test, especially for gallstones, but gives limited pancreatic detail.

  • CT: Excellent for pancreatic masses, pancreatitis complications, and staging, but less detailed for duct anatomy compared with MRCP.

Exam Pearl:
Preoperative pancreatic duct anatomy → MRCP.
ERCP = diagnostic + therapeutic, but invasive.
